result.area: Contradictions and drift across the documentation set (docs/, ops/, presentation/, README.md, CLAUDE.md, .claude/agents/)
result.summary: The re-anchoring after the SPOC confirmed 9 Sep = Day 11 was applied to five documents (CLAUDE.md header, README, 00_CANONICAL_FACTS §11-12, TEAM_TASK_GUIDE header, SANIYA_NARRATIVE_GUIDE) and to nothing else. Five of the six per-person guides — Samartha, Rohan, Samrudh, Risheeth, Rishabh — still open with "YOUR 12-DAY PLAN" and carry DAY 11 / DAY 12 headings; four of them have not been touched since 30 Aug or 3 Sep (`git log -1` per file). Every deadline those five people hold is 1-2 days late, and Gate 5 sits, in their copy, after the round has been judged. Canonical Facts itself — the declared tiebreaker — contradicts itself in four places: §14 says sub-pixel is "shipped OFF" while §6.6 says ON by default; §10 says the internal date is "TBC" 40 lines before §10 says it is confirmed; §11 says Gate 3 "is now Day 10" while its own table says Day 8; and it dates Day 5 as both 2 Sep and 3 Sep. The approved plan (`ops/PLAN_TO_9_SEP.md`) still scripts the pitch's 20-second novelty moment around "we shipped it switched off", which reversed on 3 Sep. Two judge-facing artefacts carry claims that Invariant 2 exists to prevent: Rohan's rehearsed 60-second provenance answer says M3 "gives us the infrared leg for the multi-modal case" (no such pair was ever cut) and quotes a 36x scale ratio his own spec bans. And the claim-checker agent — the safety net for exactly these problems — points at three files that do not exist and gates its blocker verdict on "Day 12". The deck content itself (`presentation/DECK_CONTENT.md`), STATUS, GATE2_EVIDENCE, MOVE2 and QA_ANSWERS §4-7 are current and clean; the drift is concentrated in the material the other five people read.

result.area: Hostile ISRO/SAC judge — attacking the deck, the Q&A bank and the novelty claim
result.summary:
This project is unusually honest about its limits — GATE2_EVIDENCE.md and QA_ANSWERS.md volunteer the 0° loss, the 45–60° blind spot, the missing cross-sensor data and the no-cast-shadow renderer. That discipline is real and it will score. But the *deck* has drifted off the *log* in exactly the place that carries the novelty, and three of the load-bearing claims do not survive an expert who opens `evaluation/results_log.csv` — which a SAC judge can do, since the team invites it.

The single most dangerous item: slide 2 of the built deck says the failing Tier D case had "88 correspondences, RANSAC consensus" and that "all three [PS metrics] look acceptable". The team's own logged row for that exact pair and method says **inlier_count 5, inlier_ratio 0.057, grid_coverage 0.078, distribution_cv 3.44** — every self-consistency metric failing by 3–10×. The premise of the entire novelty argument ("self-consistency cannot detect its own failure") is falsified by the team's own evidence, and one of their own docs (`docs/SANIYA_NARRATIVE_GUIDE.md:202`) already states the correct numbers. This is the "0.7 px" failure mode returning in a new place.

Second: the 2.88× Gate 2 headline compares the full pipeline (illumination normalisation + LoFTR + sub-pixel NCC) against **bare SIFT/ORB/AKAZE with no illumination normalisation at all** — a weaker baseline than the PS-setters' own published pipeline, which uses CLAHE + histogram matching + shadow normalisation. Worse, at 15° `ours_loftr` (0.2666) actually *loses* to SIFT (0.2466); the 2.88× exists only because sub-pixel refinement was switched on, and that switch was decided on the same metric and the same pairs the gate is scored on. The advantage is therefore attributable to the one component the deck explicitly disclaims as novel, measured against a baseline denied that component.

Third: the failure detector's verdict is reproduced **40 times out of 40** on the calibration set by a one-line rule, `inlier_ratio < 0.25`. Inside the operating envelope the deck claims (Δaz ≤ 30°) the detector has never fired once, and the "77% detection" comes entirely from 90° and 120° where the error is 240–350 m and any check would catch it.

THE FIVE HARDEST QUESTIONS

**Q1. "Slide 2 says RANSAC consensus and all three metrics acceptable. Your log says 5 inliers of 88, ratio 0.057, coverage 0.078, CV 3.44. Which is it?"**
Honest answer: the log is right. RANSAC did not reach consensus — it kept 5 of 88 and every standard metric screamed failure. The genuine finding is narrower and still worth saying: *the fit residual on the 5 survivors was near zero, so a residual-only report would have looked clean, but the inlier count and ratio were already telling us it failed.*
HAS THE ANSWER? **No.** The deck, `ops/QA_ANSWERS.md:62` and `ops/PHASE1_NOVELTY_DECISION.md:193` all assert the false version; only `SANIYA_NARRATIVE_GUIDE.md:202` is correct. Fix before anything else — this must be re-cut for Day 7, not Day 8.

**Q2. "Did SIFT get your illumination normalisation? My paper's pipeline does — CLAHE, histogram matching, shadow normalisation. Without it, what is 2.88× measuring?"**
Honest answer: no, the baselines saw raw renders. The 2.88× measures "our whole pipeline vs an unpreprocessed detector", and the team's own Gate-2-alt design already names that distinction. Also, without sub-pixel refinement our matcher loses to SIFT at 15° (0.2666 vs 0.2466).
HAS THE ANSWER? **No.** Nothing in `QA_ANSWERS.md` addresses baseline preprocessing. Cheapest fix in the project: re-run one arm of `sweep_baselines.py` with `core.illumination` applied to both images and log it, whichever way it comes out. If ours still wins, the claim becomes bulletproof; if it doesn't, better to know on Day 7 than on stage.

**Q3. "Show me one case where your independent check disagrees with the inlier ratio you say is inadequate."**
Honest answer: on the 40-pair calibration set there is none — `inlier_ratio < 0.25` reproduces `global_contradicted` 40/40. The one candidate is `pair_03_tierD` (ratio 0.59, contradicted), but it has no ground truth, and per known-issue 8 its 101×101 reference makes the cells narrower than 24 px so the per-cell area check — the actual innovation — is skipped and the whole-frame peak is used instead.
HAS THE ANSWER? **Partially, and it is the weakest part of the strongest claim.** The three-state map with an explicit *no-evidence* state remains a legitimate, well-cited system contribution; the "self-consistency can't catch this" framing is what does not hold.

**Q4. "Where is a real pair with a real sun difference? MiLOI is 321 of them, with ground truth, public code."**
Honest answer: we have none. All 40 "pairs" are renders of one 640×640 crop of one LOLA DEM, both images produced by the same Lambertian cosine law from the same gradient field, pure translation (rotation 0.0, scale 1.0), no cast shadows. And the team's own `PHASE0_RESEARCH_DAY5.md:200` calls MiLOI "a ready-made real Tier-A dataset with ground truth — the thing we said we could never get"; `STATUS.md` known-issue 5 says "Not attempted."
HAS THE ANSWER? **Half.** They state the synthetic limitation honestly in GATE2_EVIDENCE and QA — but the deck and both figures never say "DEM-rendered", and "we knew the dataset existed and didn't try it" is the answer a judge will extract. Given the freeze, the right move is not to chase MiLOI but to put "DEM-rendered, exact ground truth" on slide 4 and on fig1's footer so the honesty is visible without being asked.

**Q5. "Give me your accuracy in metres, on the imagery this problem statement is about."**
Honest answer: 0.0856 px on a **60 m/px** hillshade grid = **5.1 m**. On OHRC-class imagery (28 cm/px) we have no accuracy figure at all — only a 0.0376 px held-out residual on two crops of one frame, which is not accuracy. And scale invariance, one of three axes in the PS title, is never varied in any measurement: the only scale ratio ever run is the 6.4× Tier D case, which failed.
HAS THE ANSWER? **Partly.** Canonical Facts §7 mandates "always name the grid and give metres" — and slide 4 breaks it, printing "rmse_gt 0.0856 px" with no grid and no metres. One-line fix, and it converts a trap into a maturity signal.

THE STRONGEST SINGLE ATTACK ON NOVELTY: the whole claim rests on one real scene (`pair_03` and `pair_04` are the *same* Kaguya crop against the *same* LOLA DEM — see the two PROVENANCE.md files — so it is n=1, not two pairs), whose ground truth was itself derived by FFT global correlation, which is the fallback method being validated. The fallback is judged against truth produced by the fallback.

WHAT ALREADY EXISTS IN THE LITERATURE (from the team's own `PHASE0_RESEARCH_DAY5.md`): arXiv 2509.04775 (Singla/Amitabh/Dube, SAC — likely the PS authors) already owns illumination normalisation + common-GSD resampling as preprocessing, and owns the PS's metric list. Geo-LoFTR (arXiv 2502.09795) already evaluates a LoFTR variant on DEM renders with sun azimuth swept 0°–360°, which is this project's headline experiment. Rothenberger et al. (JPL, AIAA SciTech 2025) already publish LIMA, a correlation-based illumination-invariant lunar matcher — i.e. the fallback. Truong et al. PDC-Net already gives per-pixel correspondence confidence. And SAC's own arXiv 2604.22296 evaluates lunar simulators across Lambertian/Lommel-Seeliger/Hapke — so the judge most likely to be in the room has published on why Lambertian is the weakest choice. The defensible residue is genuinely narrow but real: the explicit three-state *no-evidence* semantics, and a lunar calibration of it. The deck should claim exactly that and nothing wider.

findings.evidence: core/pipeline.py:512-514 calls make_pair(..., rotation_deg=0.0, scale=1.0, shift_px=tuple(shift_px)) — every synthetic pair is a pure translation with no rotation and no scale. core/pipeline.py:505-507 crops the DEM to dem[:max_size,:max_size] (one 640x640 patch). The five shift values (x+12.37_y-8.63, x+12.88_y-3.85, x+9.88_y-11.68, x+7.77_y-12.42, x+18.06_y-9.12) are identical at every delta in results_log.csv. Real orbital pairs differ by in-plane rotation of tens of degrees, by scale, and by albedo contrast (maria/highlands, fresh crater rays) that has nothing to do with topography — none of which is in the experiment. And ops/PHASE0_RESEARCH_DAY5.md:200 records that MiLOI (321 real multi-illumination LROC NAC pairs, ground truth, public code at github.com/Bin501/CNSFM) is "a ready-made real Tier-A dataset with ground truth", while ops/STATUS.md known-issue 5 says "Not attempted." findings.title: The 180deg result — called "the strongest single figure in the project" — is an algebraic identity of the cosine hillshade that the project's own code deliberately excluded as flattering
findings.evidence: core/pipeline.py:467-471: "IT DOES NOT USE make_pair's DEFAULT SUNS. Those are 45 and 225 degrees - a 180-degree flip, which is a near-exact contrast inversion (Pearson -0.99), and illumination.gradient_orientation is BUILT to be invariant to exactly that. The flattering number is the default one." In evaluation/shaded_relief.py the shade is cos(ze)cos(slope) + sin(ze)sin(slope)cos(az-aspect); replacing az with az+180 negates only the second term, so a 180deg flip is an exact affine contrast inversion up to a smooth cos(slope) offset. ops/GATE2_EVIDENCE.md then presents 180deg (0.080 px, 62,519x vs SIFT) as "the strongest single figure in the project", and presentation/make_figures.py:113-115 annotates it directly on fig1.
findings.why_it_matters: The stated control — "SIFT does not recover at 180deg, so the recovery is attributable to our normalisation" — does not test what it claims. SIFT's descriptors are built on gradient magnitude and unsigned orientation histograms and are not contrast-inversion invariant by construction, so SIFT failing at 180deg is expected whether the image is a render or a photograph. The control cannot separate "our normalisation is invariant" from "our renderer produces an exact inversion". A judge from the group that published arXiv 2604.22296 on Lambertian vs Lommel-Seeliger vs Hapke lunar reflectance will go straight here, and the project's own file already wrote down why the case is flattering.
findings.how_to_verify: sed -n '464,472p' core/pipeline.py alongside sed -n '70,82p' evaluation/shaded_relief.py; then substitute az -> az+180 in the shade expression by hand.

findings.title: The Tier D ground truth was built by the same FFT global correlation the fallback uses, so the fallback is validated against truth produced by the fallback

audit_directives: Treat evaluation/results_log.csv as the only authority and diff EVERY number and every qualitative claim on the built deck against it — not against DECK_CONTENT.md, which is a draft. For any claim of the form 'metric X looked acceptable while the registration was wrong', pull the actual row and check EVERY metric in it, not the one the claim names. The critical finding here was found by reading inlier_count/inlier_ratio/grid_coverage_fraction/distribution_cv on the row the slide itself cites.

Whenever a comparison against a baseline is claimed, open the baseline runner and check what preprocessing each arm received. In this repo, baselines/sweep_baselines.py and baselines/sift_baseline.py apply no illumination normalisation while the 'ours' arm does — verify by grep for 'illum' in baselines/. result.summary:
The suite is 218 tests, 6.05 s, exit 0 (`python -m pytest -q`), and its quality is well above average for a hackathon: `core/test_pipeline_contract.py`, `core/test_pipeline_synthetic.py`, `core/test_reliability.py`, `core/test_subpixel.py` and `app/test_change_detection_scaling.py` are adversarial, each names the defect it exists to prevent, and each would genuinely fail if the code broke. There is almost no assertion padding — only 7 bare `assert x is not None` lines, all in `evaluation/test_metrics.py` where a real assertion follows.

The gaps are not in the tested modules; they are in what is not tested at all. Four production modules have zero behavioural tests and only a signature check in `core/test_interfaces.py`: `core/scale.py`, `core/ransac.py`, `core/matcher.py`, and everything under `presentation/` and `ops/` (which `pytest.ini:12` excludes from `testpaths` entirely). And the answer to "is there a test that would catch a regression in the five Gate-2 metrics?" is no — no test in this repo ever opens the real `evaluation/results_log.csv`; every reference to it is a `tmp_path` copy. Invariant 1 is enforced by human reading only.

Acting on that gap immediately: I re-derived the Gate-2 table from the log myself. All eight published `ours` medians and the 2.88× ratio reproduce exactly — the numbers are real. But the aggregation does not match the caption printed under them in six places. "Median over 5 off-grid shifts" is true for `ours` at 60–180° and for classical at 0–30°, and false everywhere else: `ours` pools 10–11 rows at 0/15/30/45° (20 exact duplicate rows, logged once by the M4 sweep and again by the reliability calibration run), and the classical arm's medians at 45° and beyond are over 2, 1, 1, 1 and 1 surviving rows. The headline 62,519× separation at 180° is the median of a single SIFT run. That is the highest-risk thing in my area, it is a test gap and a claim gap at the same time, and one 30-line test closes both.

findings.title: core/scale.py has zero behavioural tests, and its half-pixel convention is invisible to every existing test because every pair but one runs at scale factor 1.0
findings.evidence: core/test_interfaces.py:47-49 checks only the parameter names of to_common_gsd/to_original/resample. No test file imports core.scale for anything else (grep -rn 'core.scale' --include=test_*.py). core/scale.py:66-74 implements the pixel-centre inverse (x+0.5)/f - 0.5 and its own docstring says dropping the half pixel 'is the entire margin'. Measured: at factor 0.5 the correction is worth up to 0.51 px; at the 0.15625 factor the demo actually uses it is 0.5/0.15625 - 0.5 = 2.7 px on the original grid = ~25 m at Kaguya's 9.37 m/px. Crucially, reading scale_factors out of the four cached results: pair_01 (1.0,1.0), pair_00_dryrun (1.0,1.0), pair_04_tierD_native (1.0,1.0), pair_03_tierD (0.15625,1.0) — and _synthetic_pair renders both images at one GSD, so every Gate-2 pair is also 1.0. At factor 1.0 the expression (x+0.5)/1.0-0.5 is an exact identity, so deleting the half-pixel terms would change nothing on any pair except pair_03_tierD, and would be caught by no test and by no end-to-end run.
findings.why_it_matters: Scale invariance is demand #3 of the problem statement and CANONICAL_FACTS Sec.6.5 calls common-GSD resampling 'a required step, not an optimisation'. It is also the module that maps matched points back to the original grid, so a bug here biases the sub-pixel claim directly. The one pair that exercises it, pair_03_tierD, is the multi-modal leg carrying Gate-2 criterion 6 ('231 m +/- 216 m'). An untested module on the only path that produces the multi-modal number is the wrong module to leave unguarded going into a freeze.

findings.title: core/ransac.py has zero tests, and info['threshold_px'] demonstrably reports the default rather than the threshold actually used
findings.evidence: core/test_interfaces.py:52-53 checks only filter_matches/warp signatures; no test imports core.ransac otherwise. core/ransac.py:105 hardcodes "threshold_px": DEFAULT_THRESHOLD_PX inside _info(), while core/ransac.py:97 passes the real value only into the free-text note. Measured: filter_matches(src, ref, threshold_px=25.0)[3] returns {'threshold_px': 3.0, 'note': 'MAGSAC++ at 25.0 px'}. The one caller that passes a custom threshold is ops/bet_a_experiment.py:101. Separately, the module docstring (core/ransac.py:31-40) enumerates four degenerate behaviours it measured against opencv-contrib-python 5.0.0.93 — <4 points raises, identical points return (None,None), collinear return (None,None), and the (N,1) mask must be ravelled — and promises 'never raises on degenerate input'. I verified all four still behave as documented; none is pinned by a test.
findings.why_it_matters: filter_matches is on every demo path and every catalogue loop, and the docstring's whole point is that two of the four degenerate cases raise while two return None — exactly the asymmetry that regresses silently on an OpenCV bump. The threshold_px field is a small lie today (Bet A is closed) but becomes a real one the moment anyone tunes the threshold before the freeze and reads the reported value back. Pinning four documented behaviours costs about fifteen minutes.

result.area: Evidence integrity — traceability of every quoted figure to evaluation/results_log.csv, append-only enforcement, row ambiguity, and pixel/grid qualification
result.summary:
I recomputed the project's headline numbers from the CSVs rather than reading them. The good news is substantial and should be said plainly: **every Gate 2 criterion reproduces exactly.** I independently recomputed medians over 5 off-grid shifts for all 8 sun deltas × 4 metrics from `evaluation/results_log.csv` and got 0.0856 / 0.9774 / 1.0000 / 0.4006 at 15° and the whole GATE2_EVIDENCE curve to the last digit. The Move-2 detection table (50%/56%/77%/100% detection, 0%/0%/0%/9% false alarm) reproduces exactly from `core/reliability_calibration.csv`. The envelope figure reproduces exactly: 817 verified cells, median 0.12279 px = 7.367 m, 99.02% under 0.5 px, 100% under 1 px. 142.7 m = 2.378653 px × 60 m/px checks out. `231 m ± 216 m`, `88 matches`, `0 of 35 cells`, `183 / 0 / 5 / 178` all trace to named rows. I ran `presentation/make_figures.load_curves()` and fig 1 matches the deck table exactly. No row's numeric values were ever mutated in git history.

The bad news is four things that a judge, or a careful reader, can catch.

**(1) "10 of 10" is wrong and it is in three documents including a spoken Q&A answer.** At the 240 m threshold the correct figure is 7 of 7 — as MOVE2's own table one paragraph above says. **(2) The append-only invariant is factually violated in git history**, and QA_ANSWERS §7 asserts the opposite as a stage claim: 11 committed rows were later removed (9 test rows plus two real `synth_sun` SIFT measurements), and a merge re-encoded the `notes` bytes of pre-existing rows. **(3) There are two distinct `ours_loftr` experiments with identical `pair_id`, `method` and `config` and materially different values** — CANONICAL_FACTS §11 quotes one batch, QA_ANSWERS quotes the other, and a naive median over the log gives a third answer. This is exactly the "which row" ambiguity the brief asked about, and it is real. **(4) The 62,519× headline — called "the strongest single figure in the project" — rests on one successful SIFT run out of five**; the other four are `ransac_failed`, yet the table presents 4,971.7 as a median of 5.

Plus: the shipped deck quotes pixel values with no grid and no metres on slide 4, violating Invariant 2 on the actual deliverable, while slide 2 does it correctly.

findings.evidence: QA_ANSWERS.md:185 says on stage: "Every number we quote is in evaluation/results_log.csv, which is append-only — nothing is edited or deleted, including the rows that made us look worse." Git history disproves it. Commit f788a17 (Rishabh Arun, 3 Sep, 'change detection: log results and move Day 6 notes') deletes the row `2026-09-03T04:07:42.295307+00:00,test_pair_allowed,synthetic,test,...,too_few_matches`. audit_directives: Recompute, do not read. For every figure in a deliverable, load evaluation/results_log.csv or core/reliability_calibration.csv and reproduce the number with your own median/count/ratio before accepting it. In this project the summary tables are overwhelmingly correct — the defects are in the prose sentences BETWEEN the tables, which is where '10 of 10' and 'about six seconds' live.

When a number is a median, always report and check n, and check the status column. Baseline rows in results_log.csv use status='ransac_failed' with an empty rmse_gt_px; any median that silently drops those is a survivor-only statistic. Specifically check how many of the 5 repeats produced a scoreable transform for every cell of the GATE2_EVIDENCE criterion-5 table.

Treat (pair_id, method, config) as a NON-unique key. This log contains both exact duplicate rows (re-runs) and, more dangerously, two distinct experiments sharing all three fields with different values. Always group by timestamp date as well, and report when a quoted figure is reproducible only from one batch.

Check append-only against git history, not the working tree. Run `git log --numstat -- evaluation/results_log.csv` looking for non-zero deletion counts, then reconstruct the timestamp set from every rev in `git rev-list --all` and diff it against HEAD. Also compare bytes, not parsed values — a merge silently re-encoded the notes field of existing rows.

Extract text from the BUILT artefact (presentation/SIH26166_deck.pptx via python-pptx), not only from DECK_CONTENT.md. The .md is transcription-ready prose; the .pptx is what a judge sees, and its bullets are hardcoded string literals in build_deck.py with no automated tie to the CSV.

Apply the Invariant 2 grid rule mechanically: every occurrence of a number followed by ' px' in a deliverable must have the reference grid named and the metres equivalent within the same sentence or bullet. The multiplier here is 60 m/px for synthetic/Tier-D-60m rows, 9.3698731836556 m/px for pair_04_tierD_native, and 0.22977 m/px for OHRC pair_01 rows — check that the right one was used.

Distinguish 'traceable to a named derivation file' from 'in results_log.csv'. Several correct figures (0.123 px / 99.0% / 817 cells, the 77% detection rate) live only in core/reliability_calibration.csv, which reliability_calibrate.py opens in 'w' mode and therefore overwrites. Confirm each such figure still reproduces from the CURRENT contents of that file, not from a superseded population.

Read each document's own self-imposed rules and check the document against them. QA_ANSWERS.md ends with a 'Things we do not say' list that it violates three times; README.md quarantines core/bench_loftr_cpu_results.csv as unquotable and QA_ANSWERS quotes it anyway. Self-contradiction inside one file is the highest-yield search in this repo.

Cross-check the same claim across all six documents rather than auditing each in isolation. Every serious defect found here was a disagreement between two documents about one measurement (88 vs 87 matches, 0.93134 vs 0.571, 4,971 vs 4,972, 10-of-10 vs 7-of-7), not an unsupported number in a single place.

The user's instinct is right, but the cause is not what they guessed. There is **no emoji anywhere** (verified: zero codepoints above U+2000 in the code body) and **no em-dashes** (zero). The file is not sloppy — it is one of the more thoughtfully-reasoned files in the repo, with a 42-line docstring defending five real design decisions. What makes it read as "AI generated" is four measurable things:

1. **It is 100% stock Streamlit.** Nothing was chosen. H1 is 44px Source Sans; the primary button is `rgb(255,75,75)` — `#FF4B4B`, Streamlit's factory red; the "Deploy" button and hamburger are still in the top right. There is no `.streamlit/config.toml` anywhere in the repo (verified by `find`), so even the dark background is not a decision — it comes from `prefers-color-scheme: dark` on this machine and will flip to stock light on any laptop set to light mode.

2. **19 coloured alert boxes carry the load-bearing content.** `st.info`/`success`/`warning`/`error` appear 19 times. The single most important claim on the result screen — the method used — is a saturated green bar. The invariant-2 cross-sensor guard is a saturated blue bar. These are the instant template tell, and they are being used for *primary* content, not exceptions.

3. **A caption epidemic.** 23 `st.caption()` calls, 368 words — **41% of all 890 visible words** on the page, every one at 14px and `opacity: 0.6`. Body text is *also* 14px. So "explanation" and "footnote" are typographically identical apart from being dimmed, which is exactly the flat, undifferentiated, over-explained texture the user is reacting to.

4. **The type scale has a hole in it.** 44px → 28px → 14px → 14px@0.6. There is no 18–20px step, so five equally-weighted `h3` sections with six `st.divider()` rules between them give the eye no path and no sense of what matters.

**Against a projector this is worse than against a laptop, and two findings are close to disqualifying.** One result is **7.5 screens of vertical scroll** (scrollHeight 5079 / clientHeight 674) — a judge sees 13% at a time. And the swipe, which the module docstring itself calls "the single most convincing thing a viewer can see," has a **brightness step at the seam that is a pure display artifact** and reads as a failed alignment. That one is the highest-value fix in this area and it is not a styling matter.

Separately: the app currently boots on `pair_00_dryrun`, so the first thing on the projector is a yellow warning about an uncatalogued dry-run fixture; and "The five metrics" is a heading over a six-row table.

Gate 3 ("a stranger operates the UI and explains the output with nobody speaking") is Day 8 — two days out. The findings below are ordered by what threatens that gate most.

result.area: Correctness and logic in the registration engine (core/*.py)
result.summary:
I read all ten core modules, ran `python -m core.pipeline` on pair_01 (reproducing the pinned residual 0.03761504064805703 exactly) and on pair_03_tierD (fallback path), ran `pytest core/ -q` (141 passed), and wrote seven probe scripts to test conventions first-hand rather than by reading.

The engine is in better shape than I expected. Every convention I could test is CORRECT and I verified each by measurement, not by reading the comment next to it: `xcorr_peak`'s sign convention (roll(a,(5,-3)) -> (-3,5)); `scale.to_original`'s half-pixel inverse; `subpixel.refine`'s direction and accuracy (0.36 -> 0.064 px on a +0.30/-0.20 shift, 0.71 -> 0.14 px at the half-pixel worst case); `_fallback`'s translation direction (recovered (7,-5) exactly and built the right affine); the homography direction into `cv2.warpPerspective`; the raw-vs-filtered discipline (`evaluate()` really does get pre-RANSAC points). There are no mutable default arguments anywhere in core/, every division I could find is guarded, and the area check tracks true shift accurately out to 20 px with no zero-bias.

I found no bug that falsifies a number already on the record. What I did find is one structural limit in the novelty claim that is worth more than any bug (the trust layer certifies a 144 m error as "verified" on all 64 cells — I reproduced this exactly), one demo-path module whose docstring says the opposite of what ships, and one latent tiling defect that Gate 3's stranger can trigger from the uploader.

findings.title: The trust layer certifies a 144 m error as "verified" on all 64 cells — the detector has a ~2.5 reference-pixel dead zone by construction
findings.evidence:

Reproduced directly by feeding `reliability_map` a homography wrong by a known amount, with matches made consistent with the wrong H so only the area check can object:
  true error 0.0 px (  0 m)  verdict=agrees        agree_frac=1.0      verified=64
  true error 2.0 px (120 m)  verdict=agrees        agree_frac=1.0      verified=64
  true error 2.4 px (144 m)  verdict=agrees        agree_frac=1.0      verified=64
  true error 2.6 px (156 m)  verdict=agrees        agree_frac=0.59375  verified=38

audit_directives: Do not re-report the conventions I verified first-hand today — they are correct and re-checking them wastes a day of the five that remain. Verified by measurement, not by reading the comment: xcorr_peak's sign (roll(a,(5,-3)) returns (-3,5), core/reliability.py:111-128); scale.to_original's (x+0.5)/f-0.5 pixel-centre inverse; subpixel.refine's direction and magnitude (0.361->0.064 px at (+0.30,-0.20), 0.707->0.142 px at the (+0.5,+0.5) worst case, 100/100 refined, zero rejections); _fallback's translation direction and its three-point affine reconstruction (recovered (7,-5) exactly, rmse_gt_px 0.0); findHomography's src->ref direction into cv2.warpPerspective without WARP_INVERSE_MAP; and the mask.ravel() before boolean indexing at core/ransac.py:92.

The single highest-value thing an auditor can do in this area is pressure-test the trust layer's detection FLOOR, not its detection RATE. ops/MOVE2_FAILURE_DETECTION_DAY6.md reports 77% detection at a 120 m threshold with 0% false alarms; that is a rate over a population. The floor is a separate, harder number: I measured it at ~2.5 reference pixels and showed all 64 cells go `verified` at a true error of 2.4 px. Sweep true error in 0.1 px steps from 2.0 to 3.0 through reliability_map with H_true=identity and confirm the exact cliff, then convert it to metres at 60 m/px and put that single sentence in QA_ANSWERS.md. Do NOT change MAX_CELL_SHIFT_PX or add sub-pixel peak fitting to xcorr_peak — Gate 2 froze the algorithm and every calibration row in core/reliability_calibration.csv was produced under the current thresholds.

When judging whether a metric is contaminated, distinguish the two remaining semi-circular paths and do not conflate them with the Sec.7 bug that is already fixed. (a) evaluate() genuinely receives RAW pre-RANSAC matches — I confirmed this at core/pipeline.py:347 and it is pinned by core/test_pipeline_contract.py; that one is closed. (b) reliability_map's `local_inlier_ratio` (core/reliability.py:267-273) reprojects the raw matches through the SAME H that MAGSAC fitted to all of them, so it is a self-consistency measure, and it is one of the three conditions for a cell to be `verified`. This is defensible because core/reliability.py:372 also requires the independent area check and the calibration table validates the end result — but if anyone quotes `local_inlier_ratio` from reliability_calibration.csv as evidence of accuracy, that is the Sec.7 bug wearing a new hat. (c) NCC sub-pixel refinement runs BEFORE evaluate() sees the matches (core/pipeline.py:337), and its documented effect is to pull matches onto a common local peak; that mechanically improves `inlier_ratio` as well as `residual_px`. Gate 2 criterion 2 is inlier_ratio > 0.60. The Day-5-vs-Day-6 numbers (45deg: 0.3484 -> 0.5666) move roughly in proportion with rmse_gt_px (1.655 -> 1.096), so I could not show inflation — but an auditor with the DEM should measure inlier_ratio with and without refinement at 30-45deg and confirm the ratio of ratios, because the Gate 2 evidence discusses this trap only for residual_px.

Check every claim a core docstring makes about being tested, not just whether the code is right. core/matcher.py:53 says the tile-offset bookkeeping is "tested, not assumed" and there is no such test; that is how the _tiles duplication defect survived. Grep each 'tested'/'measured'/'pinned by' claim in core/*.py against the actual test files. Related: core/subpixel.py's default-state text is stale by a full reversal; sweep the other core docstrings for dated numeric claims that predate 3 Sep 2026, when both the refinement default and the reliability layer landed.

core/reliability_calibration.csv is opened with mode 'w' at core/reliability_calibrate.py:206 and the summary at :232 — a partial sweep silently replaces a full one, and this is already known issue 3 in STATUS.md. It is worse than logged: the file is written only AFTER the whole loop, and run_all can raise (see my finding 7), so an exception mid-sweep loses everything computed so far while the previous file survives — which makes it easy to believe the on-disk file corresponds to the last command you ran when it does not. Ran the full suite (218/218 pass, 5.0s), imported all 65 tracked Python modules, cross-referenced every `def`/`class` against whole-repo usage, hashed every tracked file, and checked every repo path named in every tracked `.md` and in `.claude/`.

result.name: Direction C — "Console 26166": a mission-ops readout for lunar registration
result.one_line_concept: A light-ground instrument console: a sticky state rail across the top that always says which pair, which tier, which sensors and where the result came from, then five numbered sections of hairline-ruled panels where every number is large tabular monospace and every status is a word before it is a colour.
result.rationale:
The app already behaves like an operations tool — it refuses to show `rmse_gt_px` on a real pair, it prints `n/a` rather than deriving a value, it names the tier next to the result, it distinguishes "the matcher's answer" from "what the system declared and used" (streamlit_app.py:423, 452-453). None of that is visible in the current visual layer, which is Streamlit stock: `st.title` + `st.caption`, five `st.subheader`s, three `st.metric`s, two `st.dataframe`s and coloured `st.success`/`st.warning`/`st.error` blocks. A judge sees a notebook, not an instrument. The design job is to make the discipline that is already in the code legible from eight metres.

Four decisions carry the direction:

1. LIGHT GROUND, NOT DARK. A classroom projector in ambient light delivers maybe 300:1 on-screen contrast; a dark UI's blacks lift to muddy grey and the whole thing loses its structure. Dark consoles look right on a monitor and die on a projector. Ground is a warm off-white `#F4F3EF` rather than pure white, because pure white blooms and haloes the text at high lamp brightness. Data surfaces are true white so panels read as inset instruments without needing a shadow.

2. STATUS BY POSITION AND WORD, NOT BY COLOURED BOX. Every `st.success`/`st.warning`/`st.error` becomes a "verdict rail": a 3px left rule, an uppercase monospace state word (`DECLARED`, `CONTRADICTED — FALLBACK USED`, `NO TRANSFORM`), then the existing sentence unchanged. The sentences are audited text; I am restyling them, not rewriting them. Colour is the third channel, never the first.

3. THE NUMBERS ARE THE TYPOGRAPHY. Consolas/Cascadia Mono with `tabular-nums` for every measured value, at 28px in the metric rail and 40px for the residual-in-metres figure. The five-metric `st.dataframe` at line 566 is the Gate 2 evidence and it currently renders at browser-default table size — unreadable from the third row of a classroom. It becomes a hand-laid rail: metric name, big value, threshold, and the literal word PASS or FAIL. `verdict()` (line 193) is untouched; the renderer only formats what it returns.

4. THE RELIABILITY MAP GETS THREE CHANNELS, NOT ONE. Today it is hue alone: green/amber/grey (STATE_RGB, line 80). That fails for a colour-blind judge and it fails on a projector with poor colour tracking. New scheme: (a) luminance ordering — verified is the brightest tint, weak mid, no-evidence clearly the darkest; (b) a fill pattern — verified plain, weak diagonal hatch, no-evidence dense stipple; (c) `core.reliability.ascii_map(rel)` — which already exists at reliability.py:496 and returns the 8x8 `V`/`w`/`.` picture — printed beside the image in monospace. That is a genuine reuse of the module's own output, adds no computation to the UI (design decision 1 holds), and is the channel that survives a bad projector, a photocopy, and a colour-blind reader.

Everything is ASCII. Not a style preference: this repo has already had a UTF-8 em dash re-encoded into cp1252 mojibake by a merge (`git show 9794a4d:evaluation/results_log.csv` vs HEAD). A CSS block and a set of UI labels full of `·` and `—` is one bad merge away from garbage on the projector. `-`, `|`, `>=` cost nothing and cannot be mangled.
result.why_not_ai_generated:
No gradient, no rounded corners (radius is 0 or 2px everywhere), no drop shadow, no card grid, no emoji, no icon set, no accent-coloured hero. The palette is four greys, one navy and three darkened status hues — nothing saturated, nothing that a marketing site would use. Structure comes from 1px hairlines and 2px section rules, which is how QGIS, a flight-planning tool or a SCADA screen is built, and is the opposite of the padded-card-on-soft-background look that LLM-generated UI defaults to.

Specific tells that this was designed against THIS app rather than generated from a prompt: sections are numbered 1-5 because the sidebar already numbers its steps "1 - Choose a pair" / "2 - Align" and the numbering continues rather than restarting; the state header carries a RESULT SOURCE field because line 379-382 builds a provenance string ("precomputed on this laptop ... commit ... 15.2 s of CPU") that is currently buried in a grey `st.caption` under the subheader; the frames strip labels the third panel `A->B` because the code's own caption calls it "Source, aligned onto reference"; the ASCII cell map is used because `ascii_map()` already exists and is unused by the UI; the overlay hatch is specified in numpy index arithmetic against the existing `reliability_overlay()` loop rather than as a vague "add a pattern".

And it is restrained on purpose. There is no animation, no transition, no hover effect that does anything. A judge who suspects a team of dressing up a thin result looks for polish; the defence is density and plainness — an interface that looks like it was built to be used at 2 a.m., not to be screenshotted.
result.projector_notes:
GROUND: light, decided, not a preference. Set `base = "light"` explicitly in config.toml — without a theme block Streamlit follows the OS setting, and if the demo laptop is in Windows dark mode the app inverts in front of the judges. That single line is the highest-value item in the config.

CONTRAST BUDGET: every text colour is >= 4.6:1 against its own background measured on paper, which leaves headroom for a projector that eats roughly half of it. `--c-ink #14181C` on `--c-ground #F4F3EF` is ~15:1. The tertiary label grey is `#5F666D` (~5.0:1), not the `#8A8A8A` that looks elegant on a monitor and vanishes on a screen. No status colour is lighter than `#8A5300`; there is no yellow anywhere, because saturated yellow on white is invisible under a lamp.

SIZES, minimum to maximum: 11px is the floor and is used only for uppercase letterspaced labels, which read at distance far better than their size suggests. Body 16px, captions 13px, section rules 14px, metric values 28px, the residual-in-metres hero figure 40px. Rule of thumb used throughout: a value a judge is meant to read out loud is >= 28px; a value they only need to know exists can be 13px.

WINDOW: run the demo maximised at 1920x1080 mirrored to the projector, NOT at the laptop's native scaling with the browser at 100%. If the projector is 1024x768 or 1280x800, press Ctrl+- once — the layout is `max-width: 1680px` with flex wrapping and degrades cleanly. Do not run in a half-width window: the three-frame strip collapses and the state header wraps to three rows.

WHAT TO CHECK IN THE ROOM, in this order and it takes ninety seconds: (1) stand at the back and read the residual metres figure — if you cannot, zoom in one step, not up; (2) confirm the state header is still visible after scrolling to the change-detection section (it is sticky; if the projector shows it jittering, delete the `position: sticky` line and it becomes a normal top strip); (3) look at the reliability overlay and confirm you can tell weak from no-evidence WITHOUT reading the legend — if the hatch is invisible at distance, raise `HATCH_STEP` from 6 to 8; (4) confirm the browser is not in dark reader mode and no extension is inverting the page.

LAMP AND ROOM: ask for the projector's "presentation"/"bright" picture mode, not "cinema" — cinema mode crushes the light greys the panel borders are made of. If the room lights cannot be dimmed, the light ground is the right call and nothing needs to change. If someone insists on turning the lights fully off, the app still works; it will simply look brighter than necessary.

DO NOT: hand the laptop to a judge with the browser zoomed to a level nobody tested; open devtools; or let Streamlit's "Rerunning..." toast be the last thing on screen when you stop talking.

# .streamlit/config.toml
# SIH26166 demo console. Read by `streamlit run app/streamlit_app.py` when the
# working directory is the repo root - which is how ops/ runs it. If you launch
# from elsewhere this file is IGNORED and the app falls back to the OS theme;
# that is the single most likely way the demo appears in dark mode in front of
# the judges. Launch from the repo root.
#
# Streamlit 1.62.0 (requirements.txt). Only long-standing keys are used. If a
# future version rejects one, Streamlit names the offending key on startup -
# delete that line, do not debug it five minutes before a gate.

[theme]
# base MUST be set. With no [theme] block Streamlit follows the operating
# system, and the demo laptop in Windows dark mode inverts the whole app.
base = "light"

primaryColor = "#1F4B73"              # navy - buttons, focus rings, slider
backgroundColor = "#F4F3EF"           # warm off-white; pure white blooms on a projector
secondaryBackgroundColor = "#E6E4DE"  # sidebar chassis, code blocks, table headers
textColor = "#14181C"                 # near-black, slightly cool

# "sans serif" is accepted by every version. The real family stacks are set in
# the CSS block (--f-ui / --f-mono) so that this line can never break startup.
font = "sans serif"

[client]
# Hides the Deploy button and the hamburger. A demo has nothing to deploy and
# every extra control is something a judge can click by accident.
toolbarMode = "minimal"
showErrorDetails = false              # a traceback on the projector is a lost round

[browser]
# Streamlit posts anonymous usage stats. With wifi off this cannot succeed, but
# it can still cost a DNS timeout on first paint. Gate 4 runs with wifi OFF.
gatherUsageStats = false

[server]
headless = true                       # do not try to open a second browser tab
runOnSave = false                     # nobody edits the file during the demo
# The local-source file watcher walks imported modules. With torch installed it
# reaches torch.classes and can raise on startup. The demo never edits files, so
# the watcher has no job. Turning it off also removes a whole class of restarts.
fileWatcherType = "none"

[runner]
fastReruns = true                     # cancel a superseded rerun instead of queuing it

[logger]
level = "error"                       # the terminal is sometimes visible on the projector

result.name: Reference Frame — instrument skin for app/streamlit_app.py
result.one_line_concept: The app dresses as the paper record of a measuring instrument — a light lab-report ground, hairline rules instead of cards, numbered panels, and every measured value set in Consolas next to its grid and its metres — so the screen makes the same promise the project's invariants make: this thing measures something and reports it honestly.
result.rationale:
Three decisions carry the whole design.

**1. Light ground, not dark.** The obvious read of "scientific instrument" is an oscilloscope: near-black, glowing green. That is the wrong call for this room and I want the reasoning on record. A projector cannot project black — black is whatever the screen reflects from the room lights. In a lit classroom a dark UI's background floats up to mid-grey while the thin bright text stays thin, and the effective contrast ratio collapses to something like 3:1 by the third row of chairs. A light ground does the opposite: the projector spends its full lumen output on the field, and the text is the *absence* of light, which ambient cannot brighten. Dark text on a light ground is also what every faculty judge has read on every printed paper they have ever reviewed. So the reference is not the CRT — it is the instrument's plotted output, the ENVI figure window, the calibration sheet. `#F7F7F4` ground, `#14171A` ink, 16.6:1.

**2. The type system is the whole design.** Three roles, no ornament: `Consolas` for anything measured, `Segoe UI` for anything argued, and `Consolas uppercase 12px/0.10em` for panel labels. That is it. A number in this app is visually a different *kind of thing* from a sentence, which is exactly the distinction `docs/00_CANONICAL_FACTS.md` and Invariant 1 spend all their effort making. `streamlit_app.py:37-41` already refuses to print `rmse_gt_px` where `residual_px` belongs; the skin makes that discipline visible instead of just true.

**3. The decoration budget is spent on rules, not surfaces.** `baseRadius: none`, zero box-shadows, no filled cards, no gradients. The existing app currently ships Streamlit's `stDecoration` element — a literal rainbow gradient bar across the top of the page — plus a "Deploy" button, plus pastel rounded `st.success`/`st.warning`/`st.error` boxes at lines 437/446/453. Those four things are the entire reason it reads as a web app. Killing them and replacing the alert boxes with a 4px-bar verdict strip whose status is a **word** (`DECLARED` / `FALLBACK USED` / `NO TRANSFORM`) does more for the identity than anything additive would.

Two supporting decisions. The single most important number — `residual_px` — is currently rendered at line 571 inside `st.success`, a green box. Green is a claim. A held-out fit residual is a measurement, and on Tier D the project's own history shows a confident residual sitting next to a 200px error. It becomes a neutral `.readout` band: value at 44px mono, then the grid name, then the metres, in one enforced template that renders `—` and a reason when the scale is unknown. That is the deck's slide-4 defect (`0.0856 px` with no grid, no metres) made structurally impossible in the one artefact a judge operates themselves.

And the reliability map gets a real second channel. `STATE_RGB` at line 80 is green/amber/grey — colour alone, on a projector, for a three-state claim that `core/reliability.py` argues is *not* three points on one scale. Verified gets a solid tint and a solid cell border and the letter `V`; weak gets the same tint plus a 45° hatch and the letter `W`; no-evidence gets **no tint at all** — a lightening toward the panel colour and a dotted border and a `—`. Absence renders as absence. The HTML legend repeats the identical hatch via `repeating-linear-gradient`, so the swatch and the pixels match.
result.why_not_ai_generated:
The tells of generated UI are a specific, short list, and this design is built by inverting each one.

- **No card grid.** There is not one `border-radius` above 0 and not one `box-shadow` in the block; `baseRadius = "none"` is set in config as well. Separation is done by 1px hairlines and vertical space. Nothing floats.
- **No hero, no gradient.** The top of the page is a two-line identification plate — instrument name, problem-statement number, then a row of status tags (`CPU ONLY`, `OFFLINE`, `REF GRID 60.0 m/px`, `BUILD b74b1e6`). It is a nameplate, not a headline. The CSS explicitly deletes Streamlit's own `stDecoration` gradient bar.
- **No emoji, no ✨, no ✓ decoration.** The only non-alphanumeric glyphs in the whole design are `·`, `—`, `+`, `/` and the arithmetic operators `<`, `>`, `>=` that are already in `METRICS`. PASS/FAIL are the words PASS and FAIL.
- **No three-column feature grid.** The only three-column row is the one that already exists at line 455 and it holds three *images* — source, reference, warped — which is a physical comparison, not a marketing rhythm.
- **Asymmetric, numbered sections.** Panels are labelled `01 INPUT` … `05 CHANGE DETECTION`, mono, uppercase, small, over a 1px rule that runs the full column width. Generated layouts centre things and give every section equal weight; instruments number their panels and let a panel be four lines long if that is all it has.
- **Deliberate flatness of colour.** Four signal colours total, all dark and desaturated (`#146B3C`, `#A8560A`, `#A3231E`, `#14487F`). No pastels, no tints-of-the-primary, no accent-on-accent. The accent blue appears on exactly one element — the Align button.
- **Honest false precision, removed.** `fmt()` currently prints five decimals for everything, so `inlier_ratio` shows as `0.97740`. The spec cuts each metric to its meaningful places and puts the full value in a `title=` attribute. A generated skin would have restyled the number; this one changed how many digits are true.
- **A choice with a stated cost.** Light-on-projector is argued against the more fashionable dark instrument look, and the argument is about lumens and ambient, not taste. Generated design does not pick the less-cool option and explain why.
result.projector_notes:
**Ground.** Light, and this is the load-bearing choice. A classroom projector in a lit room has no black — it has "screen at ambient". Dark themes lose their contrast to that floor; a light field does not, because the dark text is unlit screen and ambient light cannot make ink brighter. Assume the lamp is old and the room lights stay on.

**Type size.** The CSS sets `html { font-size: 17px }` — Streamlit is rem-based, so this scales every widget, gutter and control proportionally. Ship a sidebar checkbox `Projector mode` that re-injects the same block with `19px` (see layout change 14: one block, one `.replace()`, constraint respected). At 19px, body prose is ~19px and the primary readout is ~52px, which is legible from the back of a 10m room at 1080p. Do **not** rely on browser zoom as the primary mechanism — Ctrl+= is fine as a live rescue but it also scales the lunar imagery, and the images are the evidence.

**Contrast, measured.** ink `#14171A` on ground `#F7F7F4` = 16.6:1. Muted `#5A5D63` = 5.7:1. Accent `#14487F` = 8.4:1. Verified `#146B3C` = 6.0:1. result.name: Plate — the engineering-report skin for app/streamlit_app.py
result.one_line_concept: The demo stops looking like a dashboard and starts looking like a printed technical report someone happened to wire up: paper ground, numbered sections, numbered figures with captions, hairline rules instead of coloured boxes, and every measured quantity set in tabular monospace beside its grid and its metres.
result.rationale:
Three facts about this project drove every choice.

(1) The audit's findings are almost all *provenance* failures — a rate that travelled across three documents, two experiments sharing a config string, a "median" that was n=1, pixel figures with no grid. The visual language therefore has to be one whose native vocabulary is provenance: figure numbers, table captions, footnotes, a colophon. A dashboard has no grammar for "Table 1, medians over 5 off-grid shifts, rows named". A report does. The skin is not decoration here; it is the same argument the project is already making, made visible.

(2) `app/streamlit_app.py` already argues this in its own docstring — "THIS FILE COMPUTES NOTHING", `rmse_gt_px` is never shown on a real pair, the tier is printed next to the result. The file is written like a lab notebook and rendered like a Streamlit demo. I am closing that gap, not inventing a direction.

(3) Gate 3 is "a stranger operates the UI and explains the output with nobody speaking" (Canonical Facts §11). A stranger cannot explain three `st.metric` tiles. A stranger *can* read "Figure 3 — reference frame, cells marked by what the evidence supports" with a legend underneath it. Report furniture is self-documenting; dashboard furniture is not.

Ground: light, and this is not a taste call. A projector adds light; it cannot subtract it. In a lit classroom the black floor of a dark theme rises to whatever the room's ambient bounce is, and a 15:1 design collapses to about 3:1 at the back row. Light ground keeps its contrast because the bright pixels are the ones the projector is actually good at. Paper is `#FAF8F3`, not `#FFFFFF` — pure white blooms on a projector and, more practically, it would be brighter than the lunar imagery, which sits around mid-grey; the plates would read as holes punched in the page. The off-white keeps the images the brightest-contrast objects on screen, which is where the eye should go.

Type: three voices, one job each. Serif (Georgia) for the document — prose, headings, ledes. Humanist sans (Segoe UI) for the apparatus — figure captions, table headers, widget labels, the sidebar in its entirety. Mono (Consolas, tabular) for every measured quantity. That last split is doing real work: it makes "is this a number we measured or a word we wrote?" answerable at a glance from across the room, and it is exactly the distinction Invariant 1 is about. All three ship with Windows 11, so nothing is fetched and nothing degrades with the wifi off.

The reliability map gets three independent channels — fill pattern, border style, and how faded the terrain underneath is — with hue as reinforcement only. "No evidence" is rendered as the terrain *washing out*, which is what an absence of measurement should look like; "verified" is the only state that leaves the image at full contrast. Even printed on a monochrome laser the three states remain distinguishable, and their chosen colours happen to order monotonically in luminance (8.6 / 6.3 / 5.2 against paper) so a greyscale projector degrades gracefully rather than ambiguously.
result.why_not_ai_generated:
The tells of generated UI are all absent, and specifically:

- **No cards.** There is not one rounded corner, one drop shadow, or one box in the spec — `baseRadius`/`buttonRadius` are set to `none` and every radius is zeroed again in CSS. Structure is carried entirely by rules and whitespace. LLM output reaches for the card because a card requires no judgement about hierarchy; a rule requires you to decide what is above and what is below it.
- **No three-column feature grid, no hero, no gradient.** In fact the spec explicitly deletes Streamlit's own gradient — `#stDecoration` is the rainbow bar at the top of every Streamlit app and it is the single most "this is a Streamlit demo" pixel on the page.
- **`st.metric` is removed entirely.** The three big-number tiles at line 524–527 are the most recognisable dashboard idiom there is, and they are replaced with a figure legend that has more information in less space.
- **Old-style figures in the running prose.** Georgia's numerals are non-lining, so numbers inside sentences sit at x-height like lowercase letters. No template picks that. It is a deliberate consequence of "prose numbers are prose, measured numbers are data" — and it means a reader can *see* which numbers came out of `results_log.csv`, because those are the lining tabular ones.
- **Sentence-case headings, no title case, no colons-then-tagline.** "Where the alignment can be trusted" stays exactly as the author wrote it.
- **The palette is warm and slightly dirty.** `#FAF8F3` paper, `#CFC9BA` rules, `#8A4B10` ochre. Generated palettes are cool-neutral greys and a saturated indigo, because that is what every UI kit ships. This one reads as paper because the neutrals have yellow in them.
- **It commits to something unfashionable.** Numbered figures and a colophon are not what a startup landing page does. They are what a document does that expects to be checked.

There is also a negative test worth stating: nothing in the spec adds a single visual element that does not carry information. Every rule separates two things, every caption names a source, every colour has a word next to it.
result.projector_notes:
**Ground.** Light, decisively. A projector is an additive device: it makes white by emitting and black by not emitting, so in a lit room the black floor is set by ambient bounce, not by the design. A dark-ground app measured at 15:1 on the laptop lands around 3:1 on the wall, and the grey `no_evidence` cells become indistinguishable from the `weak` ones — the exact failure the accessibility constraint is about. Light ground keeps its ratios because the design's contrast lives in the pixels the projector actually drives hard. `base = "light"` is set explicitly in config so that a laptop running Windows in dark mode does not invert the app five minutes before the round; Streamlit follows the OS theme unless told not to, and that is a live demo-medic-grade failure mode.

**Not pure white.** `#FAF8F3` at roughly 94% relative luminance. Pure `#FFFFFF` blooms and haloes on classroom optics, and it would out-brighten the lunar plates, which sit around mid-grey after the 2nd–98th percentile stretch in `to_display()`. On the off-white, the images are the brightest-contrast objects on the page, which is where a stranger's eye should land first.

**Sizes are set for the back row, not the laptop.** `baseFontSize = 17` (Streamlit's default is 16). Body 17px/1.55, figure captions 14px, the small-caps apparatus labels 12px at 0.10em tracking — that tracking is not styling, it is what keeps 12px caps resolvable when the projector is soft. Section headings 25px, page title 38px. On a 1920×1080 projector at classroom distance this puts body text at roughly the angular size of 11pt print held at arm's length, which is the floor.

**One switch if the room's projector turns out to be 1024×768.** Change `baseFontSize = 17` to `19` in `.streamlit/config.toml` and change `--measure: 68ch` to `62ch` in the CSS. Nothing else moves; the layout is set in `ch` and rem-free px so it scales coherently. Test this *before* Gate 4, not during it.

**Never rely on hue at distance.** Cheap projectors compress saturated colours badly and some classroom units are visibly green-shifted. Every state in this design carries a word and a pattern; the three reliability colours were additionally chosen to order monotonically in luminance (verified 8.6:1, weak 6.3:1, no-evidence 5.2:1 against paper) so that even if colour is destroyed entirely, the three states still separate by lightness *in the right order*.

**Do not use the swipe slider from the back of the room.** The seam marker is a 2px white line (line 178). On a projector at 30 feet that is roughly one perceptible line-width; it survives, but do not shrink it. If the swipe reads poorly in rehearsal, widen the marker to 3px — it is display-only code and touches no measurement.

**Rehearse with the actual laptop plugged into the actual projector at least once before Day 9.** Specifically check: (a) that Georgia and Consolas are both present and rendering — if the sidebar suddenly looks like Times, the font stack fell through; (b) that the reliability overlay's diagonal hatch has not aliased into moiré at the projector's scaling ratio — if it has, change the hatch period from 10 to 14 in `reliability_overlay()`; (c) that the browser is at 100% zoom, because Streamlit's layout and this CSS both assume it.

**Full-screen the browser (F11) and leave the sidebar expanded.** The sidebar is the run-parameters panel and it is part of the argument — it shows the tier, the instruments, and the same-instrument warning at line 318–322, which is the Invariant 2 defence made visible while the pair is on screen.

scores.critique: The strongest reasoning of the three and the only one whose projector case is fully quantified: every colour pair has a measured ratio (ink #14171A on #F7F7F4 = 16.6:1; caution #A8560A = 4.7:1, explicitly restricted to the verdict word and a 4px bar and never body text). Choosing `st.html` over `st.markdown(unsafe_allow_html=True)` sidesteps the 4-space-indent-becomes-a-code-block trap that Direction 2 has to warn about after creating it. The single best judgement call in the whole set is removing `st.success` from the residual at line 571: green is a claim, and on pair_04 the project's own history is a confident residual sitting beside a contradicted transform. Cutting `fmt()`'s five decimals (inlier_ratio currently renders `0.97740`) while carrying full precision in `title=` is a change to what is TRUE, not to what is pretty — no template does that. Real defects: (a) the delivered SKIN constant has no `<style>` wrapper, so `st.html(SKIN)` prints CSS as text — trivial but it is shipped broken; (b) the overlay rewrite needs `import cv2`, which `app/streamlit_app.py` does not currently import (verified: imports are csv/json/pathlib/pickle/sys/tempfile/time/numpy/streamlit), and 64 cells x ~64 `cv2.line` hatch strokes plus two-pass `putText` re-run on every seam-slider drag on a 2048^2 plate — it flags this and does not fix it; (c) it recommends implementing on Day 8, and per 00_CANONICAL_FACTS.md:416 Day 8 IS Gate 3 — following its own advice puts a half-applied restyle in front of the stranger.

scores.name: Direction 2 — Plate (engineering-report skin)
scores.critique: The sharpest single argument in the set — the audit's failures are provenance failures, and a report has native grammar for provenance (Table 1, Figure 3, a colophon) where a dashboard has none. The luminance-ordered reliability states (verified 8.6:1, weak 6.3:1, no-evidence 5.2:1 against paper) are the best-reasoned accessibility scheme anyone proposed, because they degrade to greyscale in the RIGHT ORDER rather than merely remaining distinguishable. The `@media print` block is the best idea in the entire brief and nobody else has it: Ctrl+P is the fallback when the projector dies, and it produces an artefact a judge can be handed. But the metaphor over-corrects. Gate 3 is 'a stranger OPERATES the UI'; a 38px Georgia masthead, an abstract paragraph, numbered footnote lists and always-open back matter invite reading, not operating, and they add the most vertical scroll of the three inside a 3-minute pitch. Old-style figures in running prose is defended intelligently but will read to some faculty as a rendering fault, not a decision.
